lesson.title: No Compromise with Sin: William Lloyd Garrison and Immediate Emancipation
lesson.summary: William Lloyd Garrison's newspaper The Liberator and his American Anti-Slavery Society made immediate, uncompensated emancipation the abolitionist movement's rallying cry, even as his uncompromising style eventually split the cause he had built.
lesson.body:
William Lloyd Garrison was born in 1805 in Newburyport, Massachusetts, and trained as a printer, a trade that gave him the technical means to become one of the most consequential editors in American history. On January 1, 1831, he launched a weekly newspaper called The Liberator, announcing in its first issue that he would not be moderate on the subject of slavery: he would not think, speak, or write with moderation, because moderation was not appropriate when arguing against a house on fire or a woman being raped. That declaration set the tone for the paper's three and a half decade run and for the wing of abolitionism Garrison came to lead.

Garrison rejected the older antislavery tradition of gradual, compensated emancipation and colonization outright. He demanded immediate emancipation without payment to enslavers, full citizenship for freed Black Americans, and treated any hesitation on these points as complicity with sin. In 1832 he helped found the New England Anti-Slavery Society, and the following year he helped organize the American Anti-Slavery Society in Philadelphia, which became the era's leading abolitionist organization and gave structure to the immediatist movement he was building through the pages of his newspaper.

Garrison's radicalism went beyond slavery itself. He was a committed pacifist and non resistant who opposed violence even in self defense, and for years he discouraged abolitionists from voting or engaging in party politics, arguing that the Constitution itself was corrupted by its compromises with slavery. In 1854, at a Fourth of July rally in Framingham, Massachusetts, he publicly burned a copy of the United States Constitution, calling it "a covenant with death and an agreement with hell" for its protections of slavery, and he increasingly argued that the free states should dissolve their union with the slaveholding South rather than remain complicit in the institution.

These positions put Garrison at odds with other abolitionists who wanted to use elections and legislation to fight slavery, including Frederick Douglass, who had begun his career as a Garrisonian lecturer but broke publicly with him around 1851 over the value of political action and the correct reading of the Constitution. The rift illustrated a real divide inside the movement between those who saw moral suasion as the only legitimate weapon and those who wanted to build parties and win votes.

Garrison kept publishing The Liberator through the Civil War, and he lived to see the institution he had spent his life denouncing formally abolished with the ratification of the Thirteenth Amendment in December 1865. He printed the final issue of his newspaper weeks later, having outlasted the very system he began his career convinced he could not compromise with even slightly.
